maintopic: REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. CHURCH IN DEBATE ON OCTOBER 11    STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER
REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. CHURCH IN DEBATE ON OCTOBER 11    STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Last night when I was not in the chair the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) stated that when the Speaker was in the chair he had handed him a motion with regard to the Supreme Court Act. Doubtless he meant by the word "handed" that he had sent the text of a motion to me. I would assure him that the document never reached me, nor was it placed by anyone at my chair. I have caused a thorough search to be made through all the papers and documents which came to my chair yesterday, and it is not among them. What happened to it after it left the hon. member for Broadview I do not know.
I should further like to point out that I have carefully read the speech that the hon. member for Broadview made yesterday on the third reading of the Supreme Court Act, and there is no reference by him in that speech to his motion. In fact, he stated in part as follow:
I want to make only a few remarks on the motion for third reading. I do not wish to object to it any further.
Standing order 45 provides that all motions, before being put from the chair, must be moved by an hon. member and seconded by another hon. member. According to the official report of the House of Commons debates of yesterday, the motion to which the hon. member for Broadview referred last night was never moved by him, nor was it seconded by another hon. member. Accordingly it could not in any event have been put from the chair, and I am satisfied that no injustice has been done to the hon. member for Broadview. However, my main purpose in rising at this time is to assure the hon. member for Broadview that the motion which he mentioned last night was never received by the Speaker.

maintopic: REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. CHURCH IN DEBATE ON OCTOBER 11    STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
On a matter of personal privilege, by leave of the house, may I just say this. I did hand in, when the Speaker left the chair, a motion for the six months hoist. It will be noticed that in committee the Chairman told me that I could not move it, that I would have to have his consent to bring it forward or have it voted upon as an amendment. A mistake was no doubt made. I may say that you, sir, have always acted fairly in these matters. I did suggest at the time that I might have leave to recommit the bill to committee for the

He sent me down a note that I could bring it up in that way but I would have to have a vote on the clause in committee. There is no doubt that what you have said, Mr. Speaker, is quite correct. subtopic: INSPECTION, APPRAISAL, ETC.
speechtext:
1.	No. However, under the 1949 integrated plan the builder is required to transfer title to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at the floor joist stage of construction and is required to trustee with the corporation the purchaser's deposit or down payment. When the property is completed and the builder has executed a transfer of title to the purchaser, the conveyance to the corporation is then cancelled and the purchaser's down payment is paid over to the builder. Prior to release of the trusteed deposit to the builder, steps are taken to ensure that he has paid all carrying charges on the property up to date of completion, including interest on advances made under the mortgage loan, taxes and fire insurance premium; otherwise the equivalent of such carrying charges are deducted from the trusteed deposit.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDER 63 TO INCLUDE PUBLIC HEALTH, WELFARE, SOCIAL SECURITY AND HOUSING
PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDER 63 TO INCLUDE PUBLIC HEALTH, WELFARE, SOCIAL SECURITY AND HOUSING
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, standing order 63 be amended by adding after subsection 1:
(m) on public health, welfare, social security and housing, to consist of thirty-five members, ten of whom shall constitute a quorum.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed to have the opportunity of submitting this motion to the house today. In one sense it is the reward of patience, because I have had this same resolution on the order paper in each session commencing with October, 1945. This is the sixth session, and this is the first time that it has been reached with opportunity for debate.
I may say that the suggestion contained in the resolution was first offered to the government on September 27, 1945, at which time the then prime minister undertook to look into the matter and consider it.
Sir, the resolution requires some brief review of the committee structure of the house. I wish to do this briefly. I do not

Standing Committees
wish to weary the house, but I think there is some information which may be of interest particularly to the newer members.
What has happened this afternoon in the appointment of the select standing committees of the house brings this matter directly to our minds. At the present time we have in the house twelve standing committees. As well there are two joint committees of both houses. A third committee was appointed today to assist Mr. Speaker in connection with the restaurant. In what I have to say I am making no reference to the last committee. I am dealing with the standing committees, of which there are today twelve, and then the two joint committees, those on printing and the library.
When one reviews the history of the committee structure of the house, Mr. Speaker, one begins with the rules adopted by the house in 1876. At that time the rules did not set forth, as they do today in standing order 63, the list of committees. In standing order 63 we have a list of the committees, and we also have the number of members who constitute those committees, and also the quorum in each case fixed by the standing order.
In 1876 there was no list of committees set forth in the rules, but there was a reference to some of these standing committees. At that time it was apparently the practice of the house to appoint standing committees at the beginning of the session, but there was no catalogue of committees that the rules required the house to set up at each session. However, at that time three standing committees were referred to in the rules, namely, banking and commerce, railways, and a joint committee of both houses on printing. In some respects these committees thus enjoy seniority.
In 1890 a revision of the rules added reference to another standing committee, namely, that on miscellaneous private bills. In 1906 several additions were made to the list of standing committees, the number at that time being fixed at eight house committees and two joint committees on printing and the library. In 1910 three more committees were added, making eleven, and the two joint committees. These three were on marine and fisheries; on mines and minerals; and on forests, waterways and water-courses.
In their present form our rules date from the revision of 1927. The rules in this respect are today exactly as they were adopted in 1927, with the exception of one amendment that was made in 1945, which I shall mention in a moment.
The effect of the 1927 change of the rules with reference to standing committees was briefly this. First, two of the standing com-

mittees, namely that on mines and minerals, and that on forests, waterways and watercourses, were combined into the standing committee on mines, forests and waters. In the second place, a committee on industrial and international relations was added. In the third place, the rule fixed for the first time the number of members of which each committee was to consist and the number that was to constitute the quorum. At that time there were thus ten standing committees, plus the two joint committees of both houses.
One change was made in this list of committees in 1945. Hon. members of the last parliament will recall that in September, 1945, Mr. Bracken, then leader of the opposition, drew attention to the fact that the committee on industrial and international relations embraced two subjects that were not closely related, but were of such great importance as to justify the appointment of a standing committee on each. That suggestion was accepted by the prime minister, and an amendment was made in September, 1945, eliminating the committee on industrial and international relations and replacing it by two committees, one on industrial relations and another on external affairs. This brings us to the present time, with twelve select standing committees of the house and the two joint committees of both houses on printing and the library.
I make this one observation on that subject before I leave it, to draw attention to a remark of the then prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, in 1345, in dealing with the suggestion of the appointment of two standing committees, namely on external affairs and industrial relations.
On page 110 of Hansard of September 12, 1945, the prime minister said in response to the suggestion of Mr. Bracken:
If there were two separate committees, therefore, it might and I believe would improve the opportunities of hon. members to give careful study to these questions.
If I might say so, Mr. Speaker, that is the keynote of my approach to this question today. The appointment of committees of this house should be designed with that object in view, namely, to improve the opportunities of hon. members to give careful study to questions of importance coming before the house.
The resolution that I have the honor to submit to the house today will, if it is adopted, provide for the establishment of a select standing committee of the house on matters of the highest importance to all Canadians, and the appointment of that committee will improve the opportunities of hon. members to give careful study to these questions, namely, public health, welfare, social security and housing. In my submission every one

of them is a question of vast importance to all Canadians, and when the four of them are linked together, as I think may properly be done, in the scope of this committee, it offers to hon. members an improved opportunity to give careful study to these questions.
Now, sir, it is fair to ask, how is our present committee structure working? I have indicated that it has not been revised in the last 22 years. There has been just this one amendment. I have before me a table, for which I am indebted to the committee branch and the parliamentary librarian, indicating the number of meetings which each of the select standing committees has held in the past five years. I have begun with the first session of the twentieth parliament of Canada. I put the figures before the house to illustrate facts which I think are of importance. In the first place there is public business of very great importance which at the present time does not fall within the scope of any of the standing committees. In the second place, if the suggestion is made that we have enough committees now, I would answer directly by saying that some of these committees are not meeting at the present time and apparently have not met for years. If there is any question of either reducing the number or avoiding any enlargement of the number of committees, then I suggest we might very well eliminate some of the committees which do not meet today, and replace them by a committee which will meet to deal with the matters of importance set out in the proposed resolution.
The first of the select standing committees, that on privileges and elections, has not met in the last five sessions of parliament. The committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines during the past five sessions has met four, four, five, three and six times respectively. The committee on miscellaneous private bills met two, two, three, four and five times respectively. The figure I am giving in each instance is the number of meetings
Standing Committees
the committee held throughout an entire session of parliament, beginning in 1945.
We realize that the committee on banking and commerce is an active committee. We find it held 10, 20, 26, 25 and 2 meetings respectively. Turning to the public accounts committee we find that in the last five years it met once in the 1945 session, and in 1946 did not meet at all; in 1947 it met 28 times; in 1948 it did not meet, and there were two meetings in 1949.
The committee on agriculture and colonization did not meet in 1945, 1946, 1948 or 1949, but held six meetings in 1947. The committee on standing orders held one, three, six, one and three meetings respectively. The record for the committee on marine and fisheries stands at two, two and one, respectively; this committee did not meet in 1948 or 1949.
The committee on mines, forests and waters did not meet in the last five sessions. While the committee on industrial relations did not meet in 1945, it held 48 meetings in 1946, nine in 1947, nine in 1948, and failed to meet in 1949. It is one of the new committees, having been established in 1945. It can be seen that it met a need, because it was more active than most of the other committees.
The other new committee established in 1945, on external affairs, held 15, 21, 15, 9 meetings in the first four years, and none in 1949.
The committee on debates did not meet in 1945, 1946, 1947 or 1949, but held one meeting in 1948. The joint committee on printing held its meetings as follows: one, one, one and three respectively, up to and including 1948. It did not meet in 1949.
The joint committee on the library of parliament held two meetings, one in 1946-and one in 1948. In the lifetime of the preceding parliament the only meeting of that joint committee was held on July 22, 1943.

I believe it is no disparagement of other committees to say that the two committees which were established first in 1945, did fill a need in the committee organization ot the house, as evidenced by the large number of meetings they held. This points unmistakably to the fact that there is a need of modernization of the committee machinery and structure of the House of Commons. Because of the inadequacy of the committee structure there are great gaps in the allotment of public business within the scope of the various standing committees.
I do not believe that in the House of Commons, in this year of grace 1949, it should be necessary to say anything about the cardinal importance of the subjects which I suggest should be assigned to a new standing committee. In my resolution I include public health, welfare, social security, and housing. Each of them is a subject of first importance, and happily they are related. I suggest they lend themselves logically and reasonably to inclusion within the scope of reference of one committee.	.
There is no reason why the subject of housing ought not to be included within the scope of a committee studying health, welfare and social security. I am sure hon. members are aware that in Great Britain the subject of housing falls within the departmental responsibility of the minister of health. I do not believe any member of the House of Commons will contend seriously that housing is not directly related to public health, welfare and social security.
There is need of better opportunity in the house, through the machinery of the house, for the study of these subjects. There is need of provision being made so that hon. members may give careful study to these questions, again using the expression of the prime minister in 1945.
Social security is not a subject on which we have reached the end of our legislative

responsibility. It is going to present continuing problems, and it is needful that the house should undertake a comprehensive approach to this question as it pursues the study of social security problems. If I have a criticism to make of the manner in which social security questions have been approached in parliament in the past, it is that the approach has been piecemeal and has not been comprehensive. The time has come when that condition should be remedied. I see no way, apart from the assistance of a committee of this kind, in which the house would be able to undertake that comprehensive approach. Such a committee would provide an opportunity for continuous study, the gathering of information and the eliciting of opinions from responsible organizations which have studied these questions. These opportunities do not exist at the present time.
The committee organization of the house does not now admit of the calling of any person before a committee of the house to discuss questions dealing with public health, welfare, social security, and housing. It is true that when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) brings in his departmental estimates they will be considered in committee of supply. The committee of the whole house will sit here, and the minister will have one or two officials in front of his desk. He will have opportunity to confer with them in hushed whispers, and will be able to give us his opinions and also information elicited at second hand from his officials. But we are not permitted to question the officials.
It is no invasion of the principle of the responsibility of government to parliament to propose that, as in the case of the other standing committees of the house, hon. members should have an opportunity of eliciting at first hand information from these departmental officials. An opportunity should also be provided through the committee machinery

of the house to enable responsible organizations, represented by people who have made exhaustive studies of these questions and whose opinions and information would be of the greatest assistance to parliament, to come before a standing committee so as to make that information and those ideas directly available. Today if they wish to lay their information before parliament all they can do is go to the minister. What goes into the minister's files does not come before the house; we do not have access to or knowledge of submissions made by such organizations.
I am glad that the matter of national health has come, by reason of the insistence of the house and increased public interest, to be regarded with greater and greater respect, and, I hope, urgency. I hope that before this twenty-first parliament runs its course some concrete and forward step will be taken in the field of public health, something more far-reaching than we have heretofore attempted as a nation. That step should be taken in concert with the governments of the provinces. But under the present organization of the business of this house it would be impossible to give to such a measure the close and detailed study it ought to receive.
Hon. members will recall that some seven years ago a special committee of the house was set up to study the whole question of national health in Canada. There was also a special committee on social security. Those committees terminated in each case with the end of the session in which they were appointed. The fact that it was found necessary to set up special committees in the fields of social security and national health is proof abundant that a standing committee embracing those two important subjects would be of the greatest assistance to this house in the discharge of its duties and in meeting a need that is being urgently felt today.
We have been told by the government that it is intended to introduce a measure at the present session to amend the National Housing Act. I am sure the house is awaiting with interest the introduction of that measure. As a matter of fact, I think most of us wish the government would bring it down quickly. Any measure that promises assistance in solving the national housing problem ought to be brought down without a moment's delay. When the measure comes before this house I can see that it will be of the greatest assistance-unless we are to be treated as mere rubber stamps or as people whose ideas are of little interest to those bringing down the measure-if a committee is available to which the measure can be referred and in which we may obtain the views of those who are dealing with this problem in its various
Standing Committees
aspects throughout the country. In that committee the measure could be reviewed, and the result would be legislation that would be vastly superior to anything that is likely to be passed by this house if information of the kind were lacking.
Would it not be of the greatest assistance to hon. members when dealing with that measure if, for example, they could have before them the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, hear his ideas and obtain directly from him any information he may have? He is not a deputy minister, and there could not be any suggestion of an invasion of the principle of the responsibility of government in proposing that the head of a crown corporation should from time to time appear, along with his officials, before a standing committee of this house in order that the house may perform its duty in seeking firsthand information from the corporation with reference to the discharge of its responsibilities. Under our present procedure there is no opportunity for carrying out that important duty. I am sure I need not dwell further on the value the individual member of such a committee would derive in obtaining information.
I have respect for the information that hon. members possess, but I think that I am being only fair and realistic when I say that regardless of how intensive our study of particular subjects may be, it is impossible, in the time available in one lifetime, considering the other duties we must discharge, to obtain all the information available on any subject. If hon. members could have access thus to further information and research I am sure it would enable them to do a vastly superior job as members of parliament.
Far from invading the principle of responsibility I suggest that such a committee could be of great assistance to the ministers concerned, in the one case the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and in the other the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. I am sure that these ministers would appreciate receiving the considered views of those who had made an intelligent study of the problem under consideration. Any minister worthy of his office should welcome the assistance that a standing committee would be able to give.
The need for such a committee is illustrated further by the fact that there has for years been in existence under this roof an informal committee made up of members of both houses who are interested in the subject of national health. That committee does not make any attempt to go into the field of housing or social security or welfare; it deals only with health. It has no status in either

Standing Committees
house; it is simply made up of a group of interested individuals who arrange luncheons from time to time, to which the members of both houses are invited, and at which they hear papers read in relation to the subject of public health.
This committee is of limited assistance because it has no status, but the fact that such a committee has existed, informal as it may be and limited as its effectiveness has been, illustrates, and I think proves conclusively, the need for a standing committee in this field.
I should like to refer briefly to some of the observations that have been made in times past on this subject. I hope it will not be said that there are too many committees of the house. That would be a poor answer to make to a suggestion of this kind. If the need exists, the fact that there are fifteen committees today is no answer to the request that a sixteenth committee be appointed to enable this house to discharge its responsibilities with reference to the public business. If that had been the answer given by Mr. Mackenzie King in 1945; if he had said that eleven standing committees of the house and three joint committees were enough, we would not have had the two committees which were set up in 1945 and which have proven to be exceedingly useful and active. I refer to the committee on external affairs and the committee on industrial relations.
Can it be said that the existence of standing committees subtracts one iota from the principle of responsibility? I submit not. What is the difference between twelve standing committees and thirteen standing committees in respect to the principle of responsibility? Surely one more committee to deal with subjects as important as these would involve no subtraction from the principle of responsibility. If the appointment of twelve committees constitutes no invasion of the principle of responsibility, then the addition of another committee would create no subtraction from that principle.
Ten days ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), speaking for the government, agreed that another standing committee of the house should be appointed, this time on atomic energy. Why? Because atomic energy is a subject that has attained first importance, in the national as well as the international sphere. Because of that fact the government agrees that there should be another standing committee of the house, in relation to subjects pertaining to atomic energy. There was no suggestion then that that violated the principle of responsibility. If there was no violation then, there certainly is none involved in the resolution I have submitted to the house this afternoon.
IMr. Fleming.]
In the face of those facts I hope that no one will suggest that we in this house are drawing too close to the United States system instead of sticking to the principle of responsibility. If we have anything to learn from the committee structure of congress at Washington, I do not know why we should be too proud to learn it. Personally I think parliament ought to welcome the opportunity to create possible improvements in the operation of the machinery of the house wherever it can find means of doing so. If, as I urge upon the house, the addition of this committee to the machinery of the house provides that opportunity, I submit that we should welcome it.
On previous occasions the government has been asked to consider this proposal. I shall give the house one extract from Hansard which reports what was said the last time the subject was before the house. I may say that my suggestion for such a committee on this occasion was made in the course of the debate in committee of supply on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I refer to Hansard of June 11, 1948, when the present Minister of National Health and Welfare was dealing with the suggestion that there should be such a standing committee. He was reviewing some of the suggestions made by hon. members in the opening debate on the estimates of his department. At page 5141 of Hansard of that date he said:
I do not think I have now anything else to say, except that the suggestion made for the setting up of a committee dealing with both health and welfare matters is one which is receiving attention. The suggestion has much merit, and I am hoping that I shall be able to take some definite steps at a later date in connection with it.
I hope the significance of those remarks will impress the house. The Minister of National Health and Welfare, the member of the government most closely in touch with matters which would come within the scope of this proposed committee, said that the suggestion that there should be a select standing committee of the house on matters of national health and welfare, social security and housing had much merit. He adds:
. . . and I am hoping that I shall be able to take some definite steps at a later date in connection with it.
It seems to me that the resolution which I respectfully offer to the house presents an opportunity to do something definite, in the words of the minister, in connection with a matter that has much merit. It is a resolution which, in the words of Mr. Mackenzie King on September 12, 1945, will improve the opportunity of hon. members to give careful study to these questions.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDER 63 TO INCLUDE PUBLIC HEALTH, WELFARE, SOCIAL SECURITY AND HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to prolong the discussion. I merely rise to compliment the sponsor of the resolution. That is one time that he has put his talents to good use. He did an excellent job in introducing it and he put a lot of work on it. I want to give him full credit. I agree with all his arguments. For several reasons there is a great necessity for a committee such as the hon. member advocated. For example, there are ninety-two new members of the house. Many of them will not get an opportunity to speak, no matter how much they would like to do so. There are also several reasons for that being so.
The committee structure gives a member, new or old, great opportunity to learn what is going on in the country in all of its ramifications, much greater than he would have merely sitting in the house no matter how long he may remain here and how many speeches he may hear. For that reason I think it is a good opportunity to give the new members, the younger ones particularly, a chance to meet experts in every field in committee meetings. The fields that the hon. member mentioned are of the greatest importance to the Canadian people.
The question of health leaves much to be desired, despite grants to the provinces, the building of hospitals, and so on. Hospitals may be built, but unless you have money you cannot get into them. A large percentage of our population is not receiving the advantages of medical science that are available today. That is a matter that should be examined very carefully, but I shall leave any further remarks on it to my friend who was on his feet when I rose and who, as a medical doctor, is much better qualified to speak on the subject than I am.
There has been a lot of work done in committee on the question of social security. We had the Marsh report. We studied it; we studied the Beveridge report, and the New Zealand set-up. We spent months in committee on the question of social security. Witnesses were brought from all parts of Canada at great expense. It cost the government a lot of money. The Marsh report has gone to the archives to gather dust. I think it would be a good thing if the Marsh report were brought forth again and submitted to the committee that is being advocated at the present time. That report covers the whole field of social security. A lot of work has been done in the past and it should be followed up.
The federal government is making health grants to the provinces but many of the provinces are not spending the money. I think in 1948 Nova Scotia only spent about
Standing Committees
one-third of what was available. They said that plans were needed and that certain things had to be done before they could take advantage of the grants. The question of housing is tied up with the whole matter of health. I am sure that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters), who has that problem under his consideration at the present time, would welcome a subcommittee of the main committee to study it with him, do some of the work, take some of the responsibility, and assist his department. It can be done. There are hundreds of people in Canada with expert knowledge in all these fields. The machinery should be created whereby they could come here and give the government and the committee the benefit of the information they have.
I have no intention of delaying the matter at all. I merely rose to support the hon. member and compliment him for raising the matter.	.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDER 63 TO INCLUDE PUBLIC HEALTH, WELFARE, SOCIAL SECURITY AND HOUSING
speechtext:
First of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) on bringing this matter to the attention of the house. This resolution has been on the order paper-I was going to say for years-during the last session of parliament, and unfortunately we never had an opportunity to discuss it. Taking the place of a standing committee of the house, there has been a voluntary committee on health which I have found very entertaining. Meetings have been held about once every six weeks. Very often scientists have addressed us on matters concerning health or research. The trouble with such a committee is that it is not practical. Entertaining though it may be, it is not practical to gather in the members to discuss a matter of research or a highly technical matter effecting some cure. The committee is not fulfilling its purpose. The fact that it is well attended proves it is an entertaining committee and that members are anxious to attend the lectures. It reveals an interest on the part of every member of the House of Commons in the matter of health. Members realize their responsibility to their constituents regarding health and social security. They attend meetings to find out what they would like to tell their constituents and what they would like to do for their constituents.
I congratulate the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) on the attitude he has taken. He mentioned the Marsh report, however, and I intend to show that national health in this country has changed so rapidly that the Marsh report is now getting old. If such a committee were set up the ground covered by the Marsh report would have to be covered again. I said conditions in this country were

Standing Committees
changing, and I intend to show that ideas formerly held concerning national health have gone by the board. Diseases which were on the top of the list as a cause of mortality have now gone to the bottom of the list, and the whole picture has changed.
We have been through a war. It is unfortunately true that the greatest progress in research and the treatment of new diseases has been made under the stress of war. Scientists were faced with the problem of dealing with some of these situations and the whole scientific army of our nation set to work to find answers to our problems. We are still reminded of the last war, of its inhumanities and the cruelties that were perpetrated. During this post-war period we are trying to envisage a future in which the physical well-being of all people will occupy the minds of those who are striving for better conditions throughout the world.
Use should be made of the scientific knowledge accumulated in the last three centuries. A few hundred years ago the goal of those interested in the art of healing was to have physicians so well learned in the knowledge of diseases that the sick under their care got well. The thinking at that time was in terms of curing disease. There was no conception of the fact that the physical welfare of a community meant more than proper nourishment and shelter, or that under such conditions only a small part of the population could benefit from the new treatments and additional skill. During the past two decades the fight to eliminate disease and suffering has received an acceleration which was not possible in previous centuries.
In talking of this matter we are all very much aware of the discoveries of scientists like Pasteur or Lister. Bacteriologists have made tremendous advances in the discovery of viruses and the part played by insects in causing or transmitting diseases. Remarkable progress has been made in immunology, nutrition, hormones, vitamins, and some of those discoveries have been little short of miraculous. Newspapers and magazines have been filled with articles about new discoveries. Some of those articles give the public false impressions. The false impression received by the laity through these articles sometimes causes a great deal of trouble. Our laboratories, our hospitals and our physicians have been armed with new scientific equipment and drugs. They are providing services which were unknown a century ago.
The point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, is that, if this new knowledge and equipment are to be used effectively for the benefit of the whole nation, it is not sufficient to improve only the method of curing disease. Our

great objective should be to keep people well. We have the advantage of these discoveries that were made. We are positive now,'for instance, that there is no reason why any child in this country should die of diphtheria. Scientists have discovered a method of immunizing that child against this disease. The time has come, Mr. Speaker, when a coroner's inquest should be held if a child dies of diphtheria. If an accident occurs on the highway and someone is killed, a coroner's inquest is held and the whole affair investigated. A child can die of diphtheria and the only formality is a certificate signed by the attending physician. I say that when a child dies of a disease against which it could have been immunized, it should call for a coroner's inquest.
New discoveries made in other branches of medical science have broadened our idea of that remarkable thing we call life. I use the term "life" as it might be applied to the human body. Our knowledge of preventive medicine today shows it would be foolish to attempt to keep all the people well by curing disease. The advances made in preventive medicine will bring about less disease. This is the ideal towards which we should strive. As knowledge is gained in the field of public health, there should not be the call for additional hospitals and physicians. That may be a new viewpoint in this matter, but I submit, sir, it is the ideal towards which we should strive. It will cost less to keep people well and the nation will enjoy a state of health that would have been unknown a century ago. We can look forward to a new concept of health by using the discoveries already made to keep people well.
I bring these matters to the attention of the house because I believe this resolution calls for a committee of the House of Commons. These matters could be placed before that committee. When matters affecting national health are considered in this house, the consideration is limited to the few hours during which the estimates of that department are before us. Questions are asked of the minister and answers are given. No opportunity is afforded to study the broader aspects of a program of public health that would serve the nation and avoid this mortality rate. The members could learn what it means not only to cure people but to prevent people from becoming ill.
Professor Winslow of Yale university medical school, and editor of the American Journal of Public Health, gives a good definition of public health-and this is what should be before every member of this house if he had a chance to hear about it on a committee -which is as follows:
Public health is the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting physical and

mental health and efficiency through organized community efforts for the sanitation of the environment, the control of community infections, the education of the individual in principles of personal hygiene, the organization of medical and nursing service, for the early diagnosis and treatment of disease, and the development of the social machinery which will insure to every individual in the community a standard of living adequate for the maintenance of health.
I can give the house another definition- this is a shorter one and is more concise- from Webster's dictionary, in which the state of health is defined as follows:
The state of being hale or sound in body, mind or soul, especially freedom from physical disease or pain.
As to the history of movements in public health, during all the years of man's existence he has been worried about diseases which afflicted him. He spent his time and his money trying to cure and to prevent those afflictions, but he laid more emphasis on the question of cure. His efforts were doomed to disappointment because he knew nothing about the etiology of these diseases. But, sir, the whole picture has changed in the past forty years. Those diseases which I mentioned in the beginning as being at the top of the list as a cause of death forty years ago are now down at the bottom, and at the top of the list we now find diseases of adult and advanced age. Those diseases of adult and later life are now listed in the first ten causes of death. The health problems of today therefore are entirely different from those at the beginning of the century.
There are other matters affecting our population which I think should be brought before a committee. We are all aware of the high cost of hospitalization. Any of us who have been unfortunate enough to have to deal with a situation like that have found out about the tremendous cost of hospital beds and the bills which had to be paid. This puts the matter of hospitalization and relief in time of sickness beyond the financial powers of the ordinary man. The cost of hospital beds has reached a height which makes it difficult for people in the lower income brackets to pay for them. Even ward rates are now at such a height that they are equal to the cost of a private room some years ago. In seeking to obtain hospitalization and to pay for hospitalization, the public are in a difficult position. This matter again could be threshed out in a committee where the costs could be obtained from the people who have to deal with institutions.
Infant mortality in Canada has shown a sharp decline. I remember speaking in this house four years ago and calling attention to the high rate of infant mortality in Canada. Since that time the rate has gone down. This decline is due in large measure to a decrease *	45781-46
Standing Committees
in the number of deaths from diseases of infants such as diarrhoea and enteritis. Immunization against infectious disease has helped to cause the decline, by controlling communicable diseases of childhood. Whereas diphtheria was the leading cause of death forty years ago, it has now practically disappeared in centres where a campaign of immunization has been carried on. Serious illness at the childhood ages has been much reduced. Pneumonia is another example. We all remember the mortality rate of pneumonia and how it was dreaded by the populace some years ago. It once ranked high as a cause of mortality, but owing to the changes in treatment of this disease, the death rate is now about the same as that for tuberculosis. The reason for this decline is the use of important scientific discoveries, such as the sulpha drugs and penicillin. The result of all these changes has been that major illnesses and chronic invalidism now exist mainly at the older age levels. This is the result of scientific discoveries and of treatment which saved a large number of people from premature death, and which spared them from infancy to the prime of life. The leading causes of death are now those conditions common at older ages. Death from these causes in older people are now a large part of the total.
Years ago, sometime about the year 1710, Joseph Addison, the great English essayist, wrote an essay which appeared in the Spectator. He called this essay "The Vision of Mirza", which it might be of interest to the house to review, having regard to what I have been trying to say about the changes in the causes of death.
In this allegory, which Addison professes to find among certain oriental manuscripts picked up in Grand Cairo, the writer is taken into the high hills of Bagdad, where he has a symbolic vision of life. A spirit asks him what he sees, and the tale goes on:
"I see a bridge," said I, "standing in the midst of the tide." "The bridge thou seest," said he, "is human life; consider it attentively." Upon a more leisurely survey of it, I found that it consisted of three score and ten entire arches, with several broken arches, which, added to those that were entire, made up the number about an hundred. As I was counting the arches the genius told me that this bridge consisted at first of a thousand arches; but that a great flood had swept away the rest, and left the bridge in the ruinous condition I now beheld it: "But tell me further," said he, "what thou discoverest on it." "I see multitudes of people passing over it," said I, "and a black cloud hanging on each end of it." As I looked more attentively, I saw several of the passengers dropping through the bridge, into the great tide that flowed underneath it; and upon further examination, perceived there were innumerable trap-doors that lay concealed in the bridge, which the passengers no sooner trod upon, but they fell through them into the tide and immediately disappeared. These hidden pitfalls were set very thick at the entrance of the bridge,

Standing Committees
so that throngs of people no sooner broke through the cloud, but many of them fell into them. They grew thinner towards the middle, but multiplied and lay closer together toward the end of the arches that were entire.
There were indeed some persons, but their number was very small, that continued a kind of hobbling march on the broken arches, but fell through one after another, being quite tired and spent with so long a walk.
That is the story of this vision. Hon. members will note from the story that the number who dropped through at the beginning of the bridge, which would represent infantile mortality, since the hidden pitfalls were close to the entrance of the bridge, grew thinner at the middle and lay closer together toward the end of the arches which were entire. The three score and ten arches of the bridge represent the years of human life. I give you that little part of the essay of Addison to represent what is happening at the present time. Instead of the body falling off at the beginning it now falls off toward the end of the bridge.
Every party in this house is committed to some form of national health plan. We possibly do not all agree as to how this will be brought about, but we are all striving toward the one goal. There are certain facts which stand out. First is the proportion of the people in middle and later life who require treatment and attention. The second is that the chief causes of disability and death are today, and possibly will be in the future, those which are characteristic of middle and later life, the cardiovascular-renal diseases; that is the heart, kidneys and blood vessels. They are now well at the top of the list as the cause of death or as the cause of disability in mid-life and later life. Heart disease mortality, and especially coronary disease of the heart, has become all too common. It is difficult now to pick up a paper in which you do not read that somebody in the prime of life has been suddenly snuffed out by coronary disease of the heart. Science has produced early and better methods of diagnosis, but apart from the strain and the stress of life during this decade, the causes of this disease, which is apparently bringing about an increasing number of deaths, demand research. We must make provision for the treatment and the care of an increasing number of cardiac cases which cause disabilities and invalidism.
Again I say, sir, that the whole picture has changed. These matters should be before a committee where we can ask specialists, and those who are learned in these matters, why these things exist, just what we are doing about them in the way of research, and what we are doing about the increased necessity of hospitalizing these people.

I am now going to talk about cancer for a few minutes with the same object in view, namely, to show the necessity of a committee considering these matters. This is a problem with which we must deal. It presents a problem so far as research is concerned, but it presents a challenge to those who are doing research. Every year in Canada approximately 14,000 to 15,000 people die of cancer, and according to the last statistics of the disease it still stands high as a cause of death in this country. I have stated several times that these statistics show changes, but it would appear that the number of cancer cases is increasing as the span of life grows longer. We can illustrate the picture more clearly by considering the fact, or at least the probability-and this is not pleasant to think about-of eventual death from this disease. The number of cases has increased steadily, and while it may be because of the better methods of diagnosis, yet the casualties are rising. It would appear that the number of new cases is higher. People are becoming more aware of the problem and are demanding better diagnostic facilities. It is a tragedy, sir, that cases of cancer are discovered in patients at a time when little can be done. The people who are competent to deal with these cases do not get them early enough. Better diagnostic facilities would mean a great deal for many cases of cancer, if they could be diagnosed in the early stages. The treatment of early lesions under skilled care has proven to be very valuable and often results in entirely eliminating the disease. We thought at one time that there was no hope. Now we do believe that with early diagnosis there is a hope that a large percentage of these cases will get better. We must take steps to intensify any method which has been shown to be of value in holding the disease in check.
I might also point out that the people who are unfortunate enough to acquire this disease are elderly, and have to undergo a long period of invalidism and hospitalization. Many of these people have not the resources to pay for nursing and attention over a long period. This is a case where health insurance and sufficient hospital accommodation could be of great assistance in providing better care.
There is another great question facing us, namely, the problem of mental health. The average member of the House of Commons takes for granted that when a minister makes a certain statement or gives certain figures or statistics that is the end so far as he is concerned, or his connection with the estimates before the house. In the case of mental health, if we had this committee-and I bring this to you again, sir,-where every member could ask questions of these people, and

understand them, the members, irrespective of their political affiliation, could deal with the matter in a way that is not possible when it is merely brought to the attention of the house for an hour or two some afternoon. Mental health is assuming a great significance in Canada. This is a remarkable statement, but it is true. The number of beds occupied by patients suffering from mental disease, or emotional breakdowns, is nearly equal to the number of beds in all the other hospitals. Mental disease is now equal in importance to physical handicaps. I do not think that the average hon. member is aware of the significance of these two statements. We must pay more attention to the provision of hospital or institutional facilities for advanced cases, and mental hygiene must take its place in dealing with a situation such as that.
Unofficial estimates-and I have checked these as well as I could from the material at hand-show the number of the mentally ill in Canada at the present time to be 200,000, 100,000 permanent and 100,000 temporary. The word "temporary" refers to those who have probably had an emotional upset and are temporarily deranged. The health league of Canada estimates another 600,000 partly disabled, making a total of 800,000 people in Canada. The cost of mental disease in Canada is approximately $500,000,000. Statistics show that the number of people in mental hospitals is increasing faster than the general population in Canada. That is something which we should all consider. Any person within sound of my voice hearing a statement like that cannot well vote against a resolution which calls for a committee in which hon. members would study these matters and make arrangements for the treatment and hospitalization of these people in the future. It may be that the increase in the number of patients is due to more complete diagnosis. The Canada Year Book says that the number of patients in mental institutions per 100,000 of the population in 1946 was 399-5, as compared with 396-5 in 1945; 388 in 1940; 352-8 in 1933; and 305-4 in 1931. The number per 100,000 of the population in 1931 was 305-4. The number in 1946 was 399 [DOT] 5. These statistics are taken from the Canada Year Book and they are absolutely authentic.
It may be that in the consideration of these matters before a committee of the house some hon. members might feel that political affairs would enter into the discussion. Let me place on record what happened in the committee on veterans affairs. For four years that committee held meetings. I remember the former minister of veterans affairs stating in the house that this was the greatest committee 45781-461
Standing Committees
that had ever functioned, and he made highly complimentary remarks about the work accomplished.
While there might have been the occasional incident which might not fall within that description, we can forget about that. The fact is that ninety-nine per cent of the time the veterans on that committee worked for the benefit of veterans in Canada. I am sure every hon. member of the House of Commons is interested in this matter of health. Is there any reason why a committee of the house would not be of assistance to any minister holding the portfolio of national health and welfare, so as to work out arrangements and discuss health matters to the advantage of all the people in Canada?
I have mentioned mental diseases and cancer; I have referred to the changing view so far as the population is concerned, and the arrangements we will have to make in the future in order to deal with that situation. As I said in the beginning of my observations, when such enthusiasm is shown over a voluntary committee called once in six weeks to hear a scientific lecture, it seems to indicate that that is something members want to hear about and to discuss.
I have said that every political party in the house is committed to some form of health insurance. I do not agree with all of them. I have no doubt we will be told in the house about the benefits of the plan in England, or that in New Zealand. Those plans may be advocated here. Any plan, sir, that has to do with the relief of human sickness or pain is praiseworthy. We must discuss this matter in the light of what will be the best plan for all Canada.
A committee could consider these plans. As I see it, politics need not be brought into its deliberations. On such a committee we could study what has happened in England, where they have a system of state medicine. We could discuss what is happening in the United States, and consider what would be the best plan for Canada.
Those are matters of importance, matters of life and death. They are vital, so far as this nation is concerned. I am not going to discuss at length the matter of health insurance of various types.
It has become apparent, however, that some of the health insurance plans already submitted in connection with state medicine have been very costly, and in some respects have not achieved the objectives they sought to achieve in the beginning. In connection with some of them the cost has gone up at a tremendous rate. I know of no substantial group in Canada who are urging state medicine as an alternative to the present

Standing Committees
system. I know of no important exponents of state medicine, in that sense; but I think we are all committed to some form of treatment whereby people will have the advantages of the scientific discoveries of past years.
The suggested committee should have the power of discussing this plan. There should be available to all citizens in Canada a program of medical care which will provide preventive, diagnostic and curative services. This program should provide a service of a high standard under conditions satisfactory to the doctors and to the public. Such a plan should not in any way infringe upon the principles of either the medical profession, the public or any others concerned. It should be a method of accumulating funds for services required to maintain the health standards of this nation.
We cannot take on something that we cannot afford; let us be sensible about that. The United States is now in the throes of discussing some plan of that type. These matters should be discussed before a committee, so that when we do adopt a plan to which all parties in the house are committed, it may be the best we could have for this country. That matter should be fully discussed.
We will never get anywhere spending two hours in a discussion of the estimates some afternoon when there is no other government business. I appeal, sir, to the members of the house to consider these matters, and to realize that we are dealing with matters of life and death. It is shocking to think that. scientific discoveries have been made, and that we have failed in the House of Commons to approve of them, or have permitted them to become matters of political discussion-and this at a time when people are suffering and dying.
Let us have this committee; let us discuss these matters intelligently. Let us look into the question of mortality rates in Canada. Hon, members will recall that I have said there are some things that can be well handled, given the opportunity; for instance, I have in mind the immunization of a child. As I said at the beginning, a matter like that should call for a coroner's inquest, and not simply be passed over by parliament during some hour or two in an afternoon when the estimates are being considered.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDER 63 TO INCLUDE PUBLIC HEALTH, WELFARE, SOCIAL SECURITY AND HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a delight for me this afternoon to support the motion offered by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), in which he calls for an amendment to standing order 63, having for its purpose the setting up of a
[Mr. Blair.)
standing committee or committees to deal with the subjects of public health, welfare, social security and housing.
I appreciate the observations of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), who has just taken his seat. I am not as well qualified as he to speak in matters of health. By profession he is a physician, and speaks whereof he knows. At the same time I would add that the imperative need for health, welfare, social security and housing in these days makes an impact not only upon the minds of physicians but upon the minds of all people with ordinary sense.
I rise to support the resolution not only because it involves these four subjects, but because it would necessitate a change in standing order 63. In these days when we must face many problems, the committees which must deal with those problems should be an asset to any government having the responsibility of determining policy in Canada.
I am not going into the details of public health itself, but I should like to present one angle of this subject. There is quite a move on foot in other nations as well as ours to bring in what is commonly known as state medicine. Are we to assume that in connection with a subject of that kind the government is going to take full responsibility of determining policy without any parliamentary investigation? State medicine is a big issue. Some of us would oppose it on the basis that it was socialistic while others would support it because they believe, whether rightly or wrongly, that the Canadian citizen would be better cared for in matters of health through such a system. All I am saying now is that there are two opposing views in connection with that problem.
Surely the government should be willing to say: "Let us lay the subject open, let us lay it bare before the people of Canada. Let us have a parliamentary committee to which any organization, any individual or any municipal or provincial government could come to make their views known, and upon the basis of such an investigation we as a government will determine our future course and policy". I mention that as one reason for setting up a parliamentary committee.
The cost in connection with any system of public health or welfare or social security would be tremendous, and the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) has touched on this phase of the question. During last session when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) presented the government's policy with respect to social security I delivered a speech, although it was not what might be called a major speech. I asked the minister a most pertinent question. I wanted

to know if this government was going on and on and on with certain social security measures which would cost a tremendous amount of money and which in this day of apparent prosperity it might be reasonable to suppose the taxpayers of Canada could provide, and what the minister would propose in the way of financing such a program should there be a period of depression.
Surely we could have expected that a responsible minister would have projected his thinking into the future far enough to be able to say what this government or any succeeding government would do in such a case, but the minister did not answer along those lines. He gave no indication of what plans would be made to meet such huge obligations. He answered my question by saying, "Oh, well, we have always done it before, I feel confident we will always be able to do it again". Any business corporation in Canada that went out on a limb like that would be considered very unsound indeed, and yet we have the government administering what is perhaps the biggest business in the country not being able to say what they will do in the event of possible adverse circumstances facing this nation.
I am in favour of this resolution because it calls for the setting up of an additional committee to deal with these matters, but I am disappointed that the resolution does not go further. I am disappointed that it does not propose the setting up of committees to study a further number of what I would regard as very important problems facing Canada today.
Government today is not the same as it used to be. There was a day when parliament met purely as legislators. There was a day when the government administered the affairs of the country simply on the basis of the legislation that had been passed. I am not saying that in those days governments went on holiday, but all they had to do was to see that the legislation already passed functioned reasonably smoothly throughout the year. But we seem to have passed that day. Government has become big business. Government has set up all sorts of government corporations.
Parliaments have met and in their legislative responsibility have delegated tremendous powers to the government. We have become not only legislators but in a sense administrators. We are asked to take a holiday from the administrative angle of it at the close of each session. But government being big business makes it most important that everything of national importance done in this country should have the closest scrutiny.
Standing Committees
I should like to ask a question or two with regard to some of these government corporations. I am entirely in sympathy with what the hon. member for Lanark said when he asked what opportunity this parliament had to discuss these vital issues except for an hour or two on some estimate. I need to mention only one or two of these corporations, for instance Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which would be covered by this resolution which calls for a committee on housing. That particular government corporation is big business, but there is no opportunity for the details of that business to be considered by this parliament.
The minister may suggest that we can discuss it on the estimates, but I should like him to point to one estimate in that blue volume that has anything to do with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. His answer to that would be that we could discuss it on the first item, departmental administration. We know how far we would get in discussing a corporation of that kind on item No. 1 of the department. Surely a corporation that is responsible for the administration of a tremendous amount of housing in Canada should be scrutinized carefully by a parliamentary committee. I say that is only reasonable.
There are other similar matters. I believe the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) mentioned the other night that there should be a complete revision of the standing committees of the house. Take, for instance, the civil service of Canada. I believe there are in the neighbourhood of 123,000 civil servants. What opportunity have we in the house to discuss the administration of the civil service? We should have a standing committee so that any civil servant, be he office boy or the head of a department, could come and make his wants and wishes known. As legislators, how much do we know about the inner workings of the civil service? Perhaps someone will rise and say that we have an opportunity to find out. It is all very well to say that, but I assure you there are not enough hours in the day for me to read everything that comes to my desk. We all know that is the case. Why should we not have specially delegated duties imposed upon various committees? Why should we not specialize in this or that subject and leave no stone unturned in respect to any important matter that faces the country?
Then there is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. By way of licence fees it takes from the taxpayers of Canada about $5 million a year. Then it comes to parliament over and over again for loans from the consolidated revenue fund. Nevertheless there is no standing committee on radio broadcasting.

Standing Committees
In the estimates there is an item of nearly $3 million for the international shortwave station. Three million dollars is a lot of money to spend on broadcasting to the world. I know it can be said that we can discuss that on the estimates, but there should be a committee examining these matters very carefully.
The national film board requires about $2 million a year. Let me point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that the national film board, a great and powerful medium of propaganda, places before the people almost anything it pleases, using motion pictures, which not only mould people's minds but so affect their emotions that they reach decisions one way or another. On top of that there is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. To be polite, I suppose I should say that it is a powerful medium for the dissemination of information, but all information is propaganda. You can call it by a nice name if you want to.
Here are these powerful government institutions. Are we going to say that the only time we have to discuss such matters is a few minutes on the estimates, which are usually brought in in a rush near the end of the session? These subjects should be scrutinized with a great deal of care.
I said that government was big business. I must say I believe the ministers of the crown bear a tremendous burden of responsibility. I do not see how they can keep their fingers on all the details of their departments. I know it is done through an efficient organization from the man at the top down. Let us take the Department of National Revenue. If ever anything needed to undergo an overhauling it is the administration of the Income Tax Act. I cannot discuss a resolution on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), but 1 know that all over the country there is dissatisfaction with the administration of that act. I do not blame the minister entirely. He has a tremendous job on his hands.
I think ministers of the crown should welcome committees that would go into these matters and make reports in order to assist them in the determination of policy. I see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) in his seat looking at a newspaper. I know he has a tremendous responsibility. I wonder how much opportunity the house has to scrutinize in detail all that is done by the Department of Public Works. We know that last year a decision was made to move the printing bureau to Hull, and that it caused a great deal of concern. I think the minister was a bit embarrassed.

No, I did not; the minister has misunderstood me. I am not criticizing him. I am merely suggesting what might have been done, or what might be done in the future, by select or standing committees having their hands on every detail of government administration.
I believe I can conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that our democracy has become topsyturvy. First of all, governments determine their policy. Legislation is brought down and put on the doorstep of parliament. The government says, "There you are, boys; that is it. What have you got to say about it?" It does not make any difference what we have to say about it. What difference does it make? We could holler so loudly it would give the lie to the disappointing acoustics of this chamber, but it would not do any good. The government has decided. It is similar to saying, "The gods have spoken."
As I say, our democracy has become topsyturvy. That is not the manner in which the business of the country should be conducted. The government determines policy and has the last say on the matter. Members of parliament have become what the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) said, merely rubber stamps. We like to throw out our chests and say, "Well, we are members of parliament." We are members of parliament, but for what? If democracy means anything, before government policy is determined the matter should be brought before the people's representatives. This

would enable the government to ascertain what the people want and, on that basis, determine what government policy should be. The picture would then be that the people would be asking the government to do this or that. At the present time the converse is true. The government tells the people what they should have.
I am saying, Mr. Speaker, that there should be a revision of our standing committees. Those committees should have the opportunity of going into every detail and scrutinizing with the greatest care everything that is of national importance. There is another matter which I think is of tremendous importance. I know when I mention it someone is going to make a mountain out of a molehill. In the United States, for instance, the seriousness of communist forces in that country has been recognized. A committee on un-American activities has been set up. As soon as that is mentioned someone says, "Yes, and what a farce." I wonder whether it is a farce. It may have appeared to be so, but I should like to tell you that it has brought the danger of the infiltration of communistic forces into the United States to the attention of the average citizen of that country. At the moment, I do not know that I would be prepared to suggest that a committee of that sort be set up in this house. I may say that the issue is tremendously important in Canada. We are trusting that the government has the matter well in hand, and that is all we can say about it.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, every national issue that concerns the welfare of our people, whether it is the paying of income tax, whether it concerns a different way of life, whether it is a matter of security and health or whatever it is-someone mentions the atomic bomb. I do not know that we need to know a great deal about the atomic bomb, but I am going to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if two or three of them were directed at Montreal, Vancouver, Winnipeg-

A report was brought in, but prices are still going up and very little has been done about the recommendations which the committee made. Then there have been royal commissions along the same lines. It seems to me a committee was set up to study the rules of the house. There was a royal commission on prices, a royal commission on fuel, and others. The royal commission studies a matter, but usually nothing is done about its report.

Standing Committees
Why set up another committee if it is simply going to discuss matters and result in no action? If the committee is to mean anything, and I support the setting up of the committee if it will mean anything, I think the government must give some undertaking that action will be taken after recommendations are made. This resolution today calls for a committee to discuss housing. Housing is an acute problem, and I think the people of Canada want some action in the matter now. They do not want it to go to a committee and be buried there for six months or a year, then have a report back and still no action taken. I think there is that danger.
I approve this resolution in principle. If the government adopt it, I hope they will give some undertaking that they will make use of the committee and adopt some of the recommendations it makes. I know that my time is not perhaps as valuable as that of some hon. members; but I do not want to waste it again in another committee, spend months sitting on it, and then have the government just bury the report. I speak personally in this regard.

speechtext:
I should like to support this resolution and to take the opportunity of associating myself with what has been said by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and by others who have spoken in this debate. I think it must be admitted that there is a great deal of truth and merit in what has just been said by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). It seems to me that committees of this house can be of two kinds. One kind is a committee to help the government avoid responsibility; that is the kind of committee that the hon. member has just mentioned such as the prices committee, the flag committee and so on. We all regret the waste of time and money that those committees involve, and I think the protest just entered by the hon. member for Moose Jaw was fully justified.
But in addition to that kind of committee- that is the committee to help the government to avoid responsibility-there is another kind; and fortunately it can be said with a great deal of truth that the majority of the committees of this house are of that other kind, namely, the kind of committee to help the government share responsibility. This committee which the motion of the hon. member for Eglinton envisages is, I am certain, that type of committee. What he has in mind is a committee which will be available at all times to examine the various problems in the fields which he has suggested should be made the responsibility of a committee; which would be available, independently as it were, to obtain evidence and opinions on those matters,

in order to enable the members of the house to express their opinions in the light of those views; and, further, would be available as a standing committee of this house when such important legislation as the proposed bill to amend the National Housing Act is being considered in the house. If there were such a committee, then it would be, one hopes, a matter of course that such legislation would be referred to it. Then the president of Wartime Housing Limited and the president and officers of the various welfare organizations across this dominion could come before that parliamentary body and give their direct evidence; and of course it is quite impossible for them to do that in the house.
I think the hon. members who have spoken previously have outlined the advantages which would follow in the sphere envisaged by this resolution. But I also want to associate myself fully with everything the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) said just a few minutes ago. As he pointed out, the other night when the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs were being discussed I made a few brief remarks on the necessity for overhauling our committee system. It seems to me that this is another proof that the time for that overhaul is ripe; I refer to the fact that so many members, on a resolution this Wednesday afternoon, would speak in this manner and would support the motion of the hon. member for Eglinton. I should just like to mention a few more reasons which I think were omitted, if I may use that word, from the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod.
Things which in the past Canada did not seem to be immediately concerned with, and things which the Canadian government as a government were not concerned with, have since the time of confederation and since the time of the various revisions of our rules become matters in which the government is deeply involved. These are matters on which it is surely necessary that we should have committees of this house to assist in doing two things. One would be to assist the government in putting legislation through with the utmost co-operation from all members and from all parties in the house. I think that is one quite legitimate function which would be served by a committee. The second is to enable the members of the house to inform themselves on the issues involved in the legislation which is discussed in the committee, and to inform the government as to what are in fact the views held by the various sections of the country which they represent.
As has been said already, our government is in business in a big way. It is a development which some of us have regretted from

time to time, or opinions have been expressed regretting it. Some say that governments should not be in business. But it does not matter, Mr. Speaker, what your view on that subject may be, the fact is that the government is in business. It is probably correct to say that the developments that have taken place in the world and in this country in the last few years and the developments which it seems will take place in the future are such that the government cannot help getting into business, and will go on getting into business in a bigger and bigger way. That being the case, the machinery which was set up-
