The point is this. Whatever may be one's views, this government, in common with all governments in the world, is getting into business and has to deal with business problems; I do not mean merely commercial business, or business in the narrow sense of the word. The very nature of things has seemed to make it essential that the government should become more and more intimately concerned with the average everyday activities of the life of this nation. That being the case, it is a fact that the machinery devised for the conduct of the business of government many years ago is no longer adequate for conducting the business with which the government has to concern itself at the present time. I think that is the main reason why we should have an overhaul of our committee system.
If everything is to be done on the estimates, and if our only opportunity to examine what the government is doing in these different spheres is to be confined to the estimates and
Standing Committees
the committee of the whole which is called the committee of supply, and it is a committee of this whole house with 262 members, we would need thirteen months a year just to get through the estimates alone if we were really to examine these things as they should be examined. We would need to sit here solidly for those thirteen months, if we could have a year of thirteen months. The only alternative is to revise our committee system and to set up, to deal with these various problems, a number of committees to which members may be appointed, thus giving them a chance to study those subjects in which they are interested, to become informed on them and to deal with them in the detail which they merit.
I should like to mention a few matters to show that there are conspicuous gaps in our present committee system. There are such things as the judiciary. We have no committee now to which any of the constitutional measures coming before us at this session can be referred. The bill which we passed yesterday and the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for a further amendment of the constitution are cases in point. We have now in Canada a court of final resort, namely, the Supreme Court of Canada. It is in a sense a part of our constitution because it is the court of final appeal on constitutional matters. We have no committee which can deal with that aspect of the matter. There is no committee on the judiciary; there is no committee on defence. As the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) mentioned, the atom bomb is a great source of peril hanging over the nation and over the minds of the people of the nation. Whether it is regarded as a part of defence or not there should be a separate committee to deal with the matter, which has been promised. It is involved in defence. There is no committee on veterans affairs. There is no committee on housing, and that brings me back directly to the resolution which is before the house at the present time.
If I may put it this way, Mr. Speaker, enough has been said to convince any person taking a detached view of the need of this country, and taking a detached view of the opportunities available to hon. members to study these problems and of the means by which hon. members may find their opportunities, that he should not vote against the resolution so ably put forward by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming).

Mr. Speaker, ordinarily the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) would have spoken to this motion, but he is at Lake Success as

one of the Canadian delegates to the meeting of the United Nations, and as acting Minister of National Health and Welfare the responsibility has fallen on my shoulders of speaking to this motion.
I must say that from the time taken by the six hon. members of opposition groups who have spoken on the motion it began to look as if a new device was being practised in this house, and that is, that hon. members of the opposition were engaged in an endeavour to talk out their own motion.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDER 63 TO INCLUDE PUBLIC HEALTH, WELFARE, SOCIAL SECURITY AND HOUSING
speechtext: You have thirty-five minutes now.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDER 63 TO INCLUDE PUBLIC HEALTH, WELFARE, SOCIAL SECURITY AND HOUSING
speechtext:
I will not take thirty-five minutes, and at the end of my remarks I shall be ready to have a vote, if that is the wish of the house, but I hope that what I say will make that unnecessary.
Hon. members who have spoken have taken a very reasonable position, and have put forward points of view which they have expressed quietly and in a way to command respect as well as attention; but I do suggest to the house that one or two things can at once be mentioned which indicate that there are two sides to the question.
The first is that in the history he gave of the development of committees in this house the hon. member for Eglinton referred to the fact that in 22 years there has been only one change, and that was made in 1945, which I think should lead hon. members to the view that the house has not lightly disturbed the set-up of committees.
The second point which I might mention is that in the discussion of the six speakers who have preceded me it is rather noticeable that not a single one of them has referred in any way, shape or form to the practice followed in the other countries in which there are British parliamentary institutions. My belief is that the system of government which we call the British parliamentary system is the best form of government yet devised by man to regulate his affairs. The fact is, as hon. members must know, though they did not refer to it, that in no parliament of the British commonwealth, so far as I know, is there in existence any committee of the kind suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton.
In a minute or two I propose to develop the reasons why that should be so; but before doing so may I at the outset say that the suggestion made by the hon. member and the point of view which I am going to express on it have no reference to the subject matter of public health, welfare, social security and housing. I am in favour of public health; I am in favour of welfare; I am in favour of social security and I am in favour of housing;

and I do not want my remarks on the subject of this motion ever to be construed in such a way as to indicate for a second that anything I have said is in the direction of blocking further development in all these four important matters.
If there were any tendency to misunderstand the position regarding them, then I could point to the fact that possibly the reason why I should be speaking today in the place of the Minister of National Health and Welfare is that from some time in 1944 until 1946 I held that portfolio, and during that time I was responsible for the administration of the social security measures and the health measures of this government; and also as a member of the committee of the government I had a part in formulating the green book proposals which are still the most forward-looking and comprehensive plans of social security and health yet put forward in any country.
The motion is one to amend standing order 63 by adding after subsection (1) words which would create a new standing committee:
(m) on public health, welfare, social security and housing, to consist of thirty-five members, ten of whom shall constitute a quorum.
It is a motion to set up a committee and not to give Canada and Canadians a new heaven or a new earth, and I suggest that the arguments put forward by the hon. members who have spoken, all representing opposition parties, indicate clearly and unmistakably what is really in their minds. If I may put it this way, what they would like to see is what is only natural, and that is government by a committee and notably a committee of opposition members; whereas we believe in the system of government by a committee, but a committee representative of the party in power and responsible through that party to parliament and to the people as a whole. I believe that there the issue lies. Let me say at once that if this were the only committee to be suggested, or if we were to proceed only in a certain direction to a limited extent, then the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), and reinforced by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) particularly, would be very persuasive. If the committee were a committee to study a matter so as to enable members to be better informed on subjects of public importance, then it might serve a very useful purpose.
But that is not the object of the committee, as developed by the hon. members. It is very clear that what they have in mind is a committee which would be responsible for initiating legislation involving the expenditure of public funds and amounting in effect to a program of legislation to be put forward by

a committee representative of various parties, and not by the cabinet which is responsible to the crown and which under our constitution is the only group that can advise on a matter of public expenditure.
As the hon. member for Eglinton has said, this matter was first put forward in the house on December 15, 1945. At that time I was minister of national health and welfare, and made a brief reply. It was put forward again, and on April 10, 1946, Mr. Speaker ruled that the motion was out of order, on the ground that a special committee had been set up to assist him in reference to standing orders.
The suggestion was renewed on May 30, 1946, upon which occasion as reported at page 2052 of Hansard I said:
I must say that my own idea with regard to this some time ago was that there should be such a standing committee; but on considering the matter and looking into the practice in the United States and in England, I am coming to the view that it probably would be a mistake lor us to have a number of standing committees dealing with the functions of different departments, such as they have in the United States. That leads to a totally different parliamentary system, one which is very much more similar to that in force in the United States than that on which we have modeled our own parliamentary system, namely, the parliament at Westminster, where they have no functional committees. They have five standing committees, and matters are referred to one or another of the committees by Mr. Speaker. From such examination as I have made of it, and comments made in England I believe that the British procedure is the best; that the multiplication of functional committees in the United States leads to an effort by committees to administer departments. I believe that experience has shown that our system is as good as, if not better than, any in the world.

Certainly. As I have indicated, I had already changed my mind. The hon. member will not trap me in any way in that respect. I went on to say:
Therefore, on that point, on which I have an open mind, I certainly am not convinced that we should change. I think we should consider most cautiously the institution of standing committees which have a definite relationship with the department and to which estimates would regularly be referred.
But I can add that as my hon. friend knows very well, since he has followed me through Hansard, on two later occasions I indicated that the views I now hold are definitely opposed to the views he has put forward.
As I have said, the position is that in the United Kingdom, where they have a system of government on which our own is modeled, there are six standing committees lettered A, B, C, D and E, and one dealing with Scottish matters. There are no functional committees. The only matters referred to the lettered committees are legislation.
Standing Committees
The only authority bearing on the advisability of this procedure is found in Campion's An Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons, where, at page 238, he says:
The function of a standing committee is to consider and amend public bills. It is true that S.O. No. 47, permits the reference to a standing committee of "other business" as well as bills, and that in 1919 the experiment was tried of referring to a standing committee certain portions of the estimates. But this experiment is not likely to be repeated.
In other words, since 1919 the only matters referred to standing committees in the British House of Commons have been bills, and those references are made by Mr. Speaker of his own volition to one or other of the named committees.

speechtext:
If the hon. member will look into it further he will see that in Canada we sit for about the same number of days as they do in the United Kingdom. The fact that those days may be concentrated more at one season of the year than another, it seems to me-and I may be unable to follow the hon. member-has no bearing whatsoever on the point under discussion.
Further, one would have thought that if this were going to be such a panacea for governments it would have been adopted in some of the other countries which follow the British system of parliamentary government. I have in mind, for example, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and now India and Pakistan. I have had inquiries made, and I have made inquiries of representatives of these countries, and I am assured that they have no such committees.
What is more, since I have been interested in the subject of parliamentary procedure ever since entering the House of Commons, and at one time held the view that it was desirable to have such committees, I have

Standing Committees
discussed this matter with the leaders of various parties in various countries of the commonwealth; and I have found without exception that they share the view I am now putting forward, namely that the institution of functional committees of this kind, if extended, inevitably would have the effect of breaking down our representative and responsible system of government.
The hon. member for Eglinton said, "Let no one say we should not have this because they have it in the United States, and we would be getting too close to the American system." He added, "If we have anything to learn, we should not be too proud to learn from the United States." I thoroughly agree with his last remark-if we have anything to learn. While I have the greatest possible respect for the American system of government and for American institutions which, in so many ways, are similar to our own, I certainly will not acknowledge that in any respect whatever are their parliamentary or congressional systems superior to ours.
I believe that the reason for that is the historical development of the country which resulted in the system of checks and balances which they found necessary when they "cut the painter" as a consequence of the American war of independence. But we have had no need to cut the painter in that way. Our development has been orderly and peaceful and it was not necessary for us to say to the king, "We will have no more." It was never necessary for us to impose checks and balances because our development, like that of the British system, has been orderly, peaceful and progressive.
It should be made clear just what the difference is between this country and the United States. In the United States all executive power is invested in the President, not in the governor in council or in the cabinet. The President's cabinet are not elected and are not responsible to congress; they are responsible only to the President. The President is elected for a fixed term and the only way in which he and the members of his administration can have continuous association with the members in both houses of congress, and vice versa, is through the device of the congressional committee. It is before the congressional committee that the administration and its representatives put forward the legislative programs, meet objections and answer questions.
But that is not the case in Canada. Here the Prime Minister and his cabinet are appointed by the crown because the party they represent commands a majority in the House of Commons-and what a majority it is. That is because they have received the

support of the electors in a majority of divisions. The Prime Minister and his colleagues meet the members of parliament because they are also members; they meet those members every day on the floor of the house and answer questions and explain legislation. They are not separated from the members by that separation of authority which exists in the United States.
The two systems are entirely different. To pick bits out of the United States system and endeavour to introduce them here is showing a failure to understand how fundamental it is to our system of government that legislation involving the expenditure of funds should be introduced as a government measure which may or may not be referred to a committee, depending upon the will of the house. Once you set up a whole range of committees to deal with all the operations of government it becomes inevitable that those committees will endeavour to administer the affairs of the different departments and thereby remove from the government the responsibility which is theirs and theirs alone, and which is the great reason for the success of our form of government. We can be held to account in the house and in the country, but the President of the United States cannot be held to account for legislation that is introduced in consequence of a sitting of a congressional committee.
These proposals are apparently plausible and reasonable but they must be examined and scrutinized with the greatest care because they strike at the roots of the fundamental principles of parliamentary democracy as we know it in Canada. Of course it may be said that we have done it already. Of course we have. But that, subject only to the exception of the committee on external affairs, happened a long time ago. The activities of these committees have become pretty well defined. But what has been suggested today by most of the speakers is that the committee should take on itself the responsibility for laying out lines of policy involving expenditures.
Another reason why that course is objectionable is that under our system the government goes to the people, outlines its platform and either secures or does not secure the support of the people. Having been returned to office it feels that it has a mandate. Each year in the speech from the throne it lays before parliament its program for the session. Since our governments are reasonable, and I believe as intelligent and as responsible as any that can be found, that program is conceived with the idea of meeting the needs of the Canadian people with such means as the people are willing to put at the disposal of parliament for the purpose.

In other words, the art of government is the art of the possible, the art of balancing what is desirable with the means by which it can be achieved. That can be done only by a government that has a long view of the whole comprehensive picture of departmental activities. If you have one committee on social security, another on housing, another on agriculture, another on fisheries and another on defence, each initiating lines of activity and developing programs of their own, then where will you have that comprehensive program that is necessary in order to carry on the government of the country?

speechtext: Will the minister be logical and go as far as to recommend the elimination of all standing committees?

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDER 63 TO INCLUDE PUBLIC HEALTH, WELFARE, SOCIAL SECURITY AND HOUSING
speechtext:
I have indicated already that I would not do that. In conclusion may I draw to your attention in a most summary way the reasons why I think this motion should not be acceded to. In the first place a committee considering policy, administration, appropriations and expenditures would be useless unless it made recommendations to the house. Such recommendations would have to be accepted or rejected by the government after it had already arrived at a decision in respect of the very matter which was the subject of recommendation. Such a decision would have been arrived at by the government in the light of its knowledge and appreciation of the various needs of government and the means whereby those needs might be met. That is where the responsibility of the government comes in.
To the extent that a committee substituted its views for those of the government and the party to which the government is responsible, and the majority in the house to which the government is responsible, it would remove responsibility from the government.
In the second place such a committee would remove responsibility from the party supporting the government and tend to get away from the two-party system which we believe fundamental and essential to the maintenance of parliamentary democracy.
Standing Committees
In the third place it would throw out of balance the government's program for the raising of revenue and the allocation of appropriations. Fourth, it would cut directly across the fundamental principle that only the government can propose expenditure. Fifth, it would put departmental officials in the position where they would either have to agree or disagree with the minister to whom they are responsible or state that an answer could not be given as contrary to government policy, and so interfere seriously with the administration of the public service.
The hon. member who moved the motion, and I believe three out of four others who spoke, made other suggestions relative to the reorganization of the committee set-up. I must say that the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), in giving the list of fifteen committees, made out a pretty good case for the elimination of some of them because they have seldom if ever met during the last five sessions.
I suggest this is the kind of thing which could only be considered as a part of a general examination of the rules of procedure of the house. I suggest also that to consider the establishment of a single committee, when several others have been put forward by hon. members, would not be the best course to follow. While I am personally opposed to the project and would vote against it if it is put forward now, it seems to me that the best time for the matter to receive consideration would be at a moment when the rules of procedure and the structure of parliamentary committees as a whole were under consideration.
Motion (Mr. Fleming) negatived on division.
